summary: Maine is a clear 'no' for the roof rat as the rule reads today, and the reason is one missing name on a list. The Department of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife (MDIFW) sorts every captive mammal into five buckets under 12 M.R.S. ch. 723 and 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7: Unrestricted, Restricted Category 1, Restricted Category 2, Prohibited, and Unclassified. The Unrestricted Species List names 'Brown Rat - Rattus norvegicus' (the fancy rat) and 'House Mouse - Mus musculus' by exact binomial, but it does not name Rattus rattus. A species that is not on the Unrestricted, Restricted, or Prohibited list is 'Unclassified,' and 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06(4) states that 'A person may not possess any species that has not been categorized' and that an unclassified species 'will not be eligible for a permit under this chapter.' So the roof rat is not merely restricted-with-a-permit (as preliminary research assumed) and it is not on the named Prohibited list either; it sits in the Unclassified gap, which functions as a flat ban because no permit can be issued for it. Maine's 'wild animal' definition (12 M.R.S. Sec. 10001(69)) reaches a species 'wild by nature, whether or not bred or reared in captivity,' so a captive-bred, hand-tame roof rat is still treated as wildlife. There IS a pathway, but it is a list-fix, not a pet permit: Sec. 7.06(5) lets a person petition the MDIFW Captive Wildlife Technical Committee and Commissioner to categorize the species (ideally onto the Unrestricted List beside the fancy rat). Until that succeeds, keeping, breeding, selling/giving, and importing a roof rat are all prohibited. The fancy rat (R. norvegicus) is freely legal with no permit. Federal law adds a thin layer for movement/commerce: USFWS treats R. rattus as 'wildlife,' the USDA Animal Welfare Act licenses only wholesale/sight-unseen dealers (hobby and direct-to-consumer sales are exempt; lab rats of genus Rattus are excluded entirely), and the CDC bars rodents of African origin (not relevant to R. rattus, which is Asian in origin). Never release a roof rat.

kit.problem: Maine sorts every captive mammal into five tiers under 12 M.R.S. ch. 723 and the MDIFW "Wildlife in Captivity" rules (09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7): Unrestricted, Restricted Category 1, Restricted Category 2, Prohibited, and Unclassified. The state's Unrestricted Species List names "Brown Rat - Rattus norvegicus," the domestic fancy rat sold in pet shops, and "House Mouse - Mus musculus," but it does not name "Rattus rattus," the domestic roof rat. The roof rat is also not on the named Prohibited list (which targets bears, big cats, wild canids, primates, and a short list of dangerous rodents). Because it is on no list, it is "Unclassified," and the rule (09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06(4)) says "A person may not possess any species that has not been categorized" and that such a species "will not be eligible for a permit under this chapter." So a captive-bred, hand-tame pet roof rat is banned by default, and no permit can even be issued for it, while the fancy rat one species over is freely legal with no permit at all. This is not a behavioral or safety judgment about the animal; it is a gap in a list. The fancy rat already on the list is itself the wild brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), domesticated in the 19th century, and a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over.
kit.ask: Ask MDIFW to use its species-categorization process (09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06(5)) to add captive-bred domestic roof rats ("Rattus rattus") to the Unrestricted Species List, alongside the domestic Norway/fancy rat ("Rattus norvegicus") and the house mouse already on it, and in the meantime to provide a written determination of how the Department currently classifies Rattus rattus so keepers know where they stand. If the obstacle is the statute's "wild by nature" language (12 M.R.S. Sec. 10001(69)), the relevant question is domestication, not wild ancestry: the dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet Maine recognizes both as common domestic animals because what makes an animal domestic is generations bred for tameness, not the wild origin of its species. The fancy rat already on the list is itself the wild brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), domesticated in the 19th century (https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/), and a captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense, one species over. Whether a captive-bred Rattus rattus is domesticated in the same sense as the fancy rat already on the list is a question for the Department to decide; the petitioner is not asking it to assume any particular answer.
kit.branch_note: This is an AGENCY problem, not a legislative one; the lever is MDIFW, not the Legislature. No Maine statute names, bans, or singles out the roof rat. The species is simply absent from the Unrestricted Species List that MDIFW creates and amends under 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, and the five-tier framework (12 M.R.S. ch. 723) delegates the species sorting to the Department. The Department has exercised that power before and maintains a standing process for it: Sec. 7.06(5) provides for a written "Request to Review or Change the Categorization of a Species," evaluated by the Captive Wildlife Technical Committee against the criteria in Sec. 7.06(3), with the Commissioner making the final decision. So the body that created the gap can close it administratively, no bill required. The petitioner should be candid that the outcome is not assured: the same Sec. 7.06(3) criteria weigh whether the species could survive in the Maine wild and whether it harbors agents harmful to people, livestock, or native wildlife, and Maine's DACF pest and pesticide materials describe the roof rat as an invasive disease vector. A realistic ask therefore offers MDIFW two acceptable outcomes: best case, add captive-bred R. rattus to the Unrestricted List beside the fancy rat; failing that, categorize it as a Restricted (Category 2) species so that a permitted pathway at least exists rather than a flat Unclassified ban. The Legislature is a fallback only if MDIFW declines both and a keeper wants parity codified.

targets.name: Maine Department of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife (MDIFW) - Wildlife Division (Captive Wildlife)
targets.why: MDIFW owns and amends the Unrestricted Species List and runs the Sec. 7.06(5) categorization-review process. Its 'Fish and Wildlife in Captivity' page describes the five tiers (including the 'Unclassified' category) and the 'Species Categorization Requests' process, with requests mailed to the Wildlife Division, Inland Fisheries & Wildlife, 353 Water Street, Augusta, ME 04330. This is the office that can actually fix the gap, by adding R. rattus to the Unrestricted List or by categorizing it into a Restricted tier so a permit becomes possible. Ask here for the categorization-request forms and for a written determination of how R. rattus is currently classified. General inbox info.ifw@maine.gov is confirmed on the official MDIFW contact page.

targets.name: Maine State Legislature - Contact Your Legislator (House & Senate)
targets.why: FALLBACK ONLY, not the primary lever. No Maine statute names or bans the roof rat, so a bill is not needed to change an agency-maintained list; the cleanest path is the MDIFW categorization request. Use this only if MDIFW declines both to add R. rattus to the Unrestricted List and to categorize it into a permitted Restricted tier, and a keeper wants the fancy-rat/roof-rat parity codified or wants a legislator to ask the Department to act. Official 'find and contact your legislator' page for both chambers.

template.en:
To: Maine Department of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife, Wildlife Division (Captive Wildlife)
Re: Request to categorize the captive-bred domestic roof rat (Rattus rattus), ideally onto the Unrestricted Species List

Dear MDIFW Wildlife Division,

I am writing about a gap in the Unrestricted Species List under 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7. The list names "Brown Rat - Rattus norvegicus," the domestic fancy rat sold in pet shops, and "House Mouse - Mus musculus," but it does not name "Rattus rattus," the domestic roof rat. Because the roof rat is on no list, I understand it is treated as an "Unclassified" species, which Sec. 7.06(4) says a person may not possess and which is not eligible for any permit. The fancy rat one species over is freely legal. The roof rats I am writing about are bred in captivity for generations, gentle, kept entirely indoors as family pets, and never released to the wild. They are kept no differently from the fancy rat.

This is a distinction based on which species name is on a list, not on how the animal lives or any risk it poses. If the concern is the statute's "wild by nature" language (12 M.R.S. Sec. 10001(69)), the dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet Maine recognizes both as common domestic animals, because what makes an animal domestic is generations bred for tameness, not the wild origin of its species. The fancy rat already on your list is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated in the 19th century. I ask the Department to consider whether a captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense as the fancy rat already on the list; I am not asking it to assume any particular answer.

Using the species-categorization process at Sec. 7.06(5), I respectfully request that the Department add captive-bred domestic roof rats ("Rattus rattus") to the Unrestricted Species List, parallel to the domestic Norway rat and house mouse already on it. If the Department concludes that some oversight is warranted, I would ask in the alternative that it categorize the captive-bred roof rat as a Restricted (Category 2) species, so that at least a permitted pathway exists rather than a flat Unclassified ban. Please also let me know the application forms required to initiate this review, and provide a written determination of how the Department currently classifies Rattus rattus, so keepers know where they stand in the meantime.

Thank you for your time and for maintaining these lists.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your town, Maine]
[Your email / phone]

kit.confidence_notes: Verified 14 June 2026 against primary maine.gov and Maine Legislature sources, plus the Cornell LII and animallaw.info reproductions of the rule. CONFIRMED: (1) The Unrestricted Species List PDF (maine.gov/ifw/docs/unrestrictedspecies.pdf) names 'Brown Rat - Rattus norvegicus' and 'House Mouse - Mus musculus' by binomial and contains NO entry for Rattus rattus / roof rat / black rat / ship rat (verified by extracting the PDF text directly). (2) 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06(4) reads verbatim: 'A person may not possess any species that has not been categorized. Any species which has not been identified as a Prohibited, Restricted, or Unrestricted species will not be eligible for a permit under this chapter, however a request may be made to review the categorization of a species subject to section 7.06(5).' (confirmed on Cornell LII and animallaw.info). (3) Sec. 7.06(5) provides the categorization-review/petition pathway ('must be made on application forms provided by the department; applicants shall bear the burden of proof'). (4) Sec. 7.06(1) provides that unrestricted species 'may be traded by commercial pet shops.' (5) 12 M.R.S. Sec. 10001(69) defines 'wild animal' as 'a species of mammal, wild by nature, whether or not bred or reared in captivity, as distinguished from the common domestic animals' (confirmed verbatim on legislature.maine.gov). (6) The MDIFW 'Fish and Wildlife in Captivity' page describes the five tiers (including 'Unclassified'), the 'Species Categorization Requests' process, and the mailing address Wildlife Division, Inland Fisheries & Wildlife, 353 Water Street, Augusta, ME 04330, and warns not to assume animals legal in other states or online are legal in Maine. (7) The general email info.ifw@maine.gov and main line (207) 287-8000 are on the official MDIFW contact page; mailing 41 State House Station, Augusta, ME 04333-0041. (8) Maine Legislature 'Contact Your Legislator' page verified. HONEST CAVEAT: an Unrestricted outcome is not guaranteed, because Sec. 7.06(3) lets the Captive Wildlife Technical Committee weigh wild-survival capability and harmful-agent risk, and Maine DACF pest/pesticide materials describe the roof rat as an invasive disease vector; a Category 2 Restricted categorization is a plausible (more conservative) agency outcome, which is why the letter offers it as an alternative. Per OPSEC and because they are not the right contact for a list/categorization petition, only the general agency inbox and the mailed-petition address are used (no individual staff names). This is a research aid, not legal advice; a keeper should confirm current classification directly with MDIFW before acquiring an animal.

keep.why: MDIFW's Unrestricted Species List names 'Brown Rat - Rattus norvegicus' and 'House Mouse - Mus musculus' by binomial but does NOT name Rattus rattus, and R. rattus is not on the Prohibited list either. Under the five-tier scheme it is therefore 'Unclassified,' and 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06(4) provides verbatim: 'A person may not possess any species that has not been categorized. Any species which has not been identified as a Prohibited, Restricted, or Unrestricted species will not be eligible for a permit under this chapter.' So possession is unlawful AND no permit can be issued. The 'wild animal' definition (12 M.R.S. Sec. 10001(69): 'wild by nature, whether or not bred or reared in captivity, as distinguished from the common domestic animals') keeps a captive-bred, tame roof rat within MDIFW wildlife jurisdiction rather than treating it as a common domestic animal. The only lawful route to possession is to first petition MDIFW under Sec. 7.06(5) to categorize the species (best case onto the Unrestricted List beside the fancy rat).
keep.governing_law: 12 M.R.S. Sec. 10001(69) (wild animal defn); 12 M.R.S. Sec. 12152 (permit to possess wildlife in captivity); 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06(1) (unrestricted), Sec. 7.06(4) (unclassified = possession barred + permit-ineligible), Sec. 7.06(5) (categorization petition); MDIFW Unrestricted Species List (names R. norvegicus, omits R. rattus).

breed.why: Breeding (propagation) requires lawful possession plus a propagation permit, and an unclassified species is both barred from possession and ineligible for any permit under 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06(4). Because R. rattus is unclassified, there is no lawful animal to breed and no propagation permit available, so breeding is prohibited. Even the simpler commercial pathway runs through the same gate: under Sec. 7.06(1) only species on the Unrestricted List may be traded by commercial pet shops, and a DACF commercial breeder/dealer or pet-shop license (7 M.R.S. ch. 739) does not override MDIFW species classification. Federal note: the USDA Animal Welfare Act licenses only wholesale/sight-unseen dealers (hobby and direct-to-consumer sales are exempt; rats of genus Rattus bred for research are excluded from the AWA), but that federal layer cannot make a state-prohibited species lawful to breed in Maine.
breed.governing_law: 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06(4) (unclassified barred + permit-ineligible), Sec. 7.06(1) (only unrestricted species traded by pet shops); 7 M.R.S. ch. 739 (DACF pet-shop/breeder/dealer licensing, does not override MDIFW classification); federal Animal Welfare Act (USDA APHIS) for wholesale/sight-unseen dealers only.

sell_give.why: Selling, bartering, or giving away a roof rat in Maine is barred by the same unclassified-species rule. 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06(1) limits commercial pet shops and dealers to species on the Unrestricted List, and R. rattus is not on it; Sec. 7.06(4) makes possession of an unclassified species unlawful for any party, so neither a seller nor a private recipient can lawfully hold the animal. Unlike a state where only the commercial 'sale' is regulated, here the underlying possession is itself unlawful, so even a free transfer or adoption is prohibited because the recipient cannot lawfully possess the rat. (Were the species ever categorized as Restricted, an interstate Certificate of Veterinary Inspection within 30 days would attach to any transfer that involves moving the animal, but that condition is moot while possession is barred.)
sell_give.governing_law: 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06(1) (pet-shop/dealer trade limited to unrestricted species), Sec. 7.06(4) (unclassified = possession barred for all parties); 7 M.R.S. ch. 739 (DACF pet-shop/dealer licensing).

transport.why: Importing or transporting a roof rat into or within Maine is unlawful while the species is unclassified. 12 M.R.S. Sec. 12152(1-A) provides that 'a person may not import wildlife into or possess wildlife in the State or receive or possess wildlife imported into the State' without a permit, and an unclassified species cannot obtain that permit (09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06(4)). MDIFW expressly warns residents not to assume animals legally for sale in adjacent states or online are lawful to bring into Maine. If the species were ever categorized as Restricted, importation would then require a Wildlife Importation Permit (Category 2: $100 application + $27 permit) plus an interstate Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) dated within 30 days, and a Category 2 possession permit ($27 + $27, valid two years) with a one-year-husbandry / 100-hours-experience requirement and Care-and-Housing standards (Sec. 7.17). Penalty for unlawful import/possession: each day is a separate Class E crime carrying a minimum fine of $50 plus an amount equal to twice the applicable permit fee (Sec. 12152(1-A)). Federal layer: USFWS treats R. rattus as 'wildlife,' and the CDC bars rodents of African origin (R. rattus is Asian in origin, so the CDC African-rodent bar does not apply). Never release a roof rat.
transport.governing_law: 12 M.R.S. Sec. 12152(1-A) (import/possession permit; Class E crime, $50/day + twice the permit fee); 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06(4) (unclassified = permit-ineligible), Sec. 7.11(1)C (import health certificate/CVI for restricted species), Sec. 7.17 (care/housing); MDIFW captivity guidance (out-of-state/online warning); federal CDC/USFWS for international.

restrictions.summary: Default ban via the 'Unclassified Species' rule. Because R. rattus is on none of MDIFW's lists, 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06(4) makes it unlawful to possess and ineligible for any wildlife permit. There is no pet-permit application a keeper can file today; the only lawful route is to first get the species categorized (next entry). Unlawful possession/import is a Class E crime, each day a separate offense, minimum $50/day plus twice the applicable permit fee (12 M.R.S. Sec. 12152(1-A)).
steps: Understand that no possession or import permit can be issued for R. rattus while it is unclassified.
Do not acquire or import a roof rat into Maine until the species is categorized; doing so is a per-day Class E crime and the animal can be confiscated.
Check local county/municipal ordinances as well; towns may further restrict animal keeping even if the species is later categorized.
restrictions.where_to_file: Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife (MDIFW), Wildlife Division

restrictions.summary: Categorization petition (the only pathway). 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06(5) lets a person petition MDIFW to review and categorize an unclassified species. The request is made on Department forms, the applicant bears the burden of proof, the Captive Wildlife Technical Committee evaluates it against the Sec. 7.06(3) criteria, and the Commissioner decides. Best outcome is adding captive-bred R. rattus to the Unrestricted List beside the fancy rat; a plausible conservative outcome is a Category 2 Restricted placement (then a Category 2 possession permit becomes available). Only after a successful categorization can any possession/import permit be sought.
steps: Request the 'Request to Review or Change the Categorization of a Species' application form from the MDIFW Wildlife Division (info.ifw@maine.gov or by mail).
Compile biological, ecological, and husbandry evidence supporting the requested category (you bear the burden of proof under Sec. 7.06(5)).
Mail the completed application to: Wildlife Division, Inland Fisheries & Wildlife, 353 Water Street, Augusta, ME 04330.
If categorized as Category 2 Restricted, then apply for a Wildlife General Possession Permit (Cat 2) and, for any import, a Wildlife Importation Permit (Cat 2) plus a CVI dated within 30 days.

Wildlife Importation Permit Application - Category 2 Restricted Species ($100 application + $27 permit)

restrictions.where_to_file: Wildlife Division, Inland Fisheries & Wildlife, 353 Water Street, Augusta, ME 04330 (categorization request); fees payable to 'Treasurer, State of Maine'.
restrictions.fees: Categorization request: no fee stated on the captivity page. Post-categorization Category 2 possession permit: $27 application + $27 permit (valid two years). Category 2 importation permit: $100 application + $27 permit.

restrictions.summary: Interstate Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI). This would apply only IF the species were categorized as Restricted and an import permit issued: 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.11(1)C and the Cat 2 import/possession forms require an interstate health certificate / CVI issued by a veterinarian licensed in the state of origin, dated within 30 days of taking possession, with disease test results approved by the Maine DACF and DHHS. It is moot while the species is unclassified and possession is barred.
steps: Applies only after a successful categorization to Restricted and issuance of a Category 2 import permit.
Then: obtain a CVI from a veterinarian licensed in the origin state, dated within 30 days of taking possession, including required disease statements.

forms.name: Wildlife Importation Permit Application - Category 2 Restricted Species (CVI requirement on the instructions page)

restrictions.where_to_file: CVI issued by a veterinarian licensed in the state of origin; filed with the MDIFW import permit. Maine DACF / DHHS approve required disease statements.
restrictions.fees: No state fee for the CVI; the issuing veterinarian charges an examination/paperwork fee.

restrictions.summary: Never release a roof rat into the wild. R. rattus is treated as an invasive species and disease vector in Maine (DACF pest/pesticide materials list 'Roof rat (Rattus rattus)' as a target pest), and releasing captive wildlife is unlawful. Rehome responsibly. Local county/municipal ordinances can further restrict animal keeping.

inquiry_focus: Under 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, the Unrestricted Species List names 'Brown Rat - Rattus norvegicus' and 'House Mouse - Mus musculus' but not Rattus rattus, and R. rattus is not on the Prohibited list, so it appears 'Unclassified' under Sec. 7.06(4) (possession barred, permit-ineligible). (1) Does MDIFW confirm that a captive-bred, domesticated Rattus rattus kept as an indoor pet is currently Unclassified (and therefore prohibited), or does the Department treat it differently? (2) Will MDIFW accept a Sec. 7.06(5) request to categorize captive-bred R. rattus onto the Unrestricted List beside the fancy rat, and what forms/evidence does it require? (3) Is there historical precedent for the Captive Wildlife Technical Committee granting Unrestricted status to a commensal rodent, or would the roof rat's pest/vector status push it toward Category 2 Restricted or Prohibited? (4) If categorized as Category 2 Restricted, does MDIFW in practice issue possession permits to private companion-pet keepers who meet the experience and caging standards, or are those permits reserved for exhibitors/researchers? (5) What is the expected timeline for a categorization decision?
